journey.title: Contract risk: every contract scored, and watched every morning
journey.prompt: I need to monitor the risk of all the contracts in our portfolio. Work out what the important risk factors and signals are from everything we have connected, and help me build the scorecard: what to measure, how to score it and how much each thing counts. Then watch every contract, and tell me when the risk of one goes up, why, and what we should do about it at that site.

reads.res: Operations data hub (214 tables), the contract repository (2,460 documents), three shared mailboxes and the public web
300 active operations and maintenance projects in five regions, $1,375.4M a year, booked under 267 profit centers and running 425 facilities. I give each project one score

reads.tool: look for a scoring template you already use
reads.res: None is connected. I found your Contracting Policy (the non-negotiable terms), three loss reviews and the monthly KPI pack, but nothing that says what to score and how. Upload yours, or I propose one

reads.tool: read the contracts you lost or left since 2021
reads.res: 7 contracts: 3 lost at renewal, 2 taken in-house, 2 ended early. What came first in each: a new client lead (5 of 7), margin under budget (7 of 7), in-house operation on a public agenda (both in-house losses)
richstatespoorstates.org (state liability ranking, 2026 edition) · EPA ECHO (permits) · FEMA flood maps · council and board agendas · municipal bond ratings

Not everything is recorded by project. Finance figures are booked by profit center, compliance and maintenance by facility, the client survey by client account. I say how each one is brought to the project and ask you to confirm

questions.title: Do you have a scoring template?
questions.text: A file with your factors and their weights, the signals in each factor, and how each signal scores 1 to 4. If you have one I use it exactly as written. If not, I propose a scorecard. Either way it appears on the right once you answer.

tiles.s: Use our factors, weights and rules as written
From what is connected and the contracts already lost

questions.title: This is how every project will be scored
questions.text: The scorecard is on the Plan tab: every factor with its share of the final score, every signal with its weight and its rule for 1 to 4. Drop a signal, add one to a factor, add a factor, or change a weight or a rule, there or here in the chat. The preview shows what each change does to your projects.

tiles.t: Score on it as it stands now
tiles.s: You can change it at any time, also after the goal is live

questions.title: The data check: a few assumptions need your call
questions.text: I tested every signal against the connected data. Most are ready. Some figures do not sit at project level (profit center, facility, client account), and one signal has no source. The data check on the plan lists each signal, how it is measured, and the assumptions I would make to get one figure per project.

tiles.t: Confirm the assumptions as they stand
tiles.s: Or change any of them on the plan first

extraDocs.took: 16 factors and 77 signals, with weights and a rule for 1 to 4 on each; used as written

nodes.title: Read every signal again and re-score
nodes.purpose: Which contracts changed, and by how much.
nodes.how: Every signal of every contract read again from its source and scored on your bands; factor scores from your weights; the contracts whose readings changed, with the old and the new score.
nodes.check: Each score recomputes from its signals, bands and weights.

nodes.title: Read the evidence behind each change
nodes.purpose: Why it changed, and what the contract says about it.
nodes.how: The message, document, row or page behind each changed reading; then the agreement: liability, who pays for the fix, how the client can leave.
nodes.check: Every change points at a dated message, row or page.

nodes.title: Weigh what is at stake and where it is heading
nodes.purpose: Which of the contracts that rose come first.
nodes.how: Annual revenue, margin, months to a decision and how the contract can end, beside the risk; the twelve-month direction of each score; anything I read that your scorecard does not score.
nodes.check: What is at stake never changes the risk score unless you asked for it.

nodes.title: Write the mitigation plan for each site
nodes.purpose: One action for every signal at 3 or 4 that can be moved, for that site.
nodes.how: For each site: the action, written from the reading, the mail about it, the contract clause and what is public; the owner from the contract master, a date, and the score the plan would bring the project to. Facts of the site are listed, not actioned.
draws: The contract master: who owns each contract
nodes.check: Every action names the signal it answers, an owner and a date.

nodes.title: Build the deliverables, act and tell you
nodes.purpose: Build what was agreed at set-up, take the actions that run by themselves, hold the others for your OK, and tell the people you chose.
nodes.how: The dashboard refreshed; then each rule that applies: tell the people named, build the deck on why it moved, write the plan. A rule set to "ask me first" waits for your OK.
draws: Your rules on the Plan tab
nodes.check: Only your rules run. Nothing is sent outside the company.

recs.title: Run the full plan at every contract that rose: an odor plan at Harlow Creek, a renewal plan at Ashby Falls, cover at Red Mesa
recs.summary: Harlow Creek: an odor source survey, load-out moved to mornings, the complaint calls returned and the Regional VP in front of the City Manager before the 8 December council. Ashby Falls: the Regional VP meets the new DPW Director before 2 December and the renewal plan starts now. Red Mesa: both posts covered from the West float pool on Monday and the sampling schedule given a second owner.
recs.tradeoff: Three regions get work this week, one of them for a contract that still rates 2.

story.text: The watch fired: three contracts changed overnight. What should be done about each?
Read the demand letter and the complaint log for Harlow Creek.
Read the agreement: liability is capped, consequential damages are not waived, odor capital is the City's.
Harlow Creek crosses from 2 to 3 on your scorecard.
Red Mesa shows the pattern that came before five of seven notices of violation.
Ashby Falls puts in-house operation on its 2 December agenda, seven months before the contract ends.
Act on all three now: one because it moved, two because the record says what comes next.

recs.title: Plans only where a rating moved; list the rest in the Monday digest
recs.summary: Follow the ratings strictly: a contract that moved up gets the full plan today. A contract that rose inside its rating goes into the Monday digest.
recs.tradeoff: Simple to explain, since it follows the ratings. But the Ashby Falls board meets on 2 December, the same day as the review, and Red Mesa goes on with one licence holder working weekends.

story.text: What if only a rating change triggers work?
The Ashby Falls board discusses in-house operation on the day of the portfolio review.
Faithful to the scorecard, and late for the two it does not yet see.

recs.title: Tell the owners now and decide the rest at the 2 December review
recs.summary: Tell the people who own each contract this morning. Take the contracts to the leadership team on 2 December and decide the plans there.
recs.tradeoff: The least work now. It uses 13 of the 30 days the letter gives, and the Ashby Falls board meets on the same day as the review.

story.text: What if the decisions wait for the leadership team?
The claims procedure asks for Legal within one working day and the insurer within 30.
The review is 12 days away; the letter gives 30.
Allowed by the procedure, costly for the odor plan and for Ashby Falls.
